rows.title: Accounting with QuickBooks and Excel
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the functions of pre-programmed general ledger accounting package.
Save, retrieve, adjust, correct, and modify data files.
Demonstrate the program's operation and application.
Produce integrated accounting reports.
Apply special functions of the program -depreciation, payroll, inventory.
Read selected reports to determine net income, balances, and variances.
Produce functional spreadsheets.
Write practical mathematical formulas to maximize spreadsheet effectiveness.
Display proper spreadsheet report format.
Interpret special applications and capabilities of Excel spreadsheets.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and record changes in assets, liabilities, and owners' equity.

Complete the steps in the accounting cycle for service and retail merchandising businesses including the following: a) prepare a balance sheet, income statement, and statement of owners' equity; b) determine and define balances of T-accounts having entries recorded on both sides of the account; c) present the fundamental accounting equation with T-account form; d) prepare a trial balance; e) record a group of transactions in a two-column general journal format and post entries; f) complete a worksheet; g) prepare an income statement, a statement of owners' equity, and a balance sheet directly from the worksheet; h) journalize and post adjusting entries and; i) journalize and post closing entries; j) prepare a post-closing trial balance and interim financial statements.
Employ information technology to accomplish the preceding tasks.

rows.title: Survey of Art from Prehistory to the Medieval Era
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: When shown an image of a major work of art, the student will correctly identify the name, country or place of origin and date.
When asked to analyze the difference between two major works or aft, the student will effectively compare and contrast styles and themes portrayed.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Objectives:
Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from prehistory to the medieval era employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious,historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from prehistory to the medieval era.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Identify major works of art and architecture from ancient times to the Middle Ages.
Compare and contrast the styles and themes portrayed in a variety of works of art and architecture.
Evaluate and critique works of art based on historical context, subject matter, theme, form, composition, material, technique, line, color, space, mass, volume, perspective, proportion, and scale.
Recognize patterns and themes presented in the history of art and architecture.
Analyze images of art and architecture from a historical as well as aesthetic perspective.

rows.title: Business Computations
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Process and interpret information to arrive at logical conclusions to common business math applications.
Apply mathematics skills to solve business math problems.
Describe the important role that mathematics plays in all facets of the business world.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Add, subtract, multiply, and divide whole numbers
Add, subtract, multiply, divide negative and positive numbers
Add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions, mixed numbers and decimals
Use orders of operations to evaluate expressions (including those with parenthesis, whole numbers powers, and perfect roots)
Use variables and combine like terms

Identify, distinguish between, appropriately use and demonstrate the following properties with integers: a. commutative, associative and distributive properties, b. additive and multiplicative inverses, c. identities elements of addition and multiplication, d. properties of one (1) and zero (0)
Understand and use checking accounts and prepare a bank statement reconciliation
Solve simple single variable first degree equations
Use equations to solve business related problems
Convert between decimals and percents and fractions and percents
Use percentage formulas and proportions to solve business problems involving percents
Develop and revise business invoices
Calculate single and series trade discounts, cash discounts and terms of sale
Calculate and evaluate mark-up and mark-on based on cost or selling price
Calculate and evaluate mark-down and mark-off based on cost or selling price
Calculate gross earnings, incentive pay plans, payroll deductions, employer's payroll expenses and self-employed person's tax responsibility
Calculate simple interest for loans with specified terms and use the simple interest formula to find principal, rate or time values
Calculate compound amount and compound interest and present values of a future amount
Calculate the present value of an annuity, future value of an annuity, sinking fund payment, and amortization payments
Calculate finance charges and new balances on charge accounts, credit cards, and lines of credit
Calculate finance charges, annual percentage rates, and amount of payoff and monthly payment amounts for installment loans
Calculate the closing costs, monthly payments, total interest, and PITI of both fixed-rate and adjustable-rate mortgages
Calculate the closing costs, monthly payments, and total interest for home equity loans and lines of credit

rows.title: Voice and Diction
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
demonstrate the ability to read an excerpt for a play, news copy or other text using proper voice and diction
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
demonstrate the ability to read an excerpt for a play, news copy or other text using proper voice and diction
compare and contrast the major dialects used in stage speech
demonstrate the ability to speak through and listen to accented speech
compare and contrast the various dialects and accen
demonstrate the ability to match nonverbal movements in synchronous motion with selected vocal dynam
distinguish and properly articulate different types of vowels and consonants
demonstrate proficient use of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)
demonstrate pitch, rate, volume and timbre appropriate to the meaning of a text
describe the effects of pitch, rate and timbre on the perception of spoken messages
identify the basic structure, function and influences on human speech and language
describe the anatomy and physiology associated with voice production
analyze their own voice and use this knowledge to aid in improving vocal qualities

rows.title: Introduction to Elementary Education
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will identify the various philosophies of education and explain their application and impact on American education
Students will describe the emergence of educational education in history and describe its impact on teaching and learning
Students will identify the responsibilities of the general public, state and federal government, and local school to provide education, and the challenges with meeting those responsibilities.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Express an understanding of the teaching profession related to historical influences, philosophical trends, educational theory, and preparation of the teacher.
Identify and explain the central issues in history and development of American education.
Students will identify the principle laws and court decisions that guide current practice
Explain how schools are governed, influenced, and financed.
Identify the components of a quality educational program and environment.
Explain strategies and ethical responsibilities to support diversity, equality and antiracism within the classroom.
Describe personal motives and values for teaching.
Summarize and critique readings relevant to issues in education such as contemporary issues, safety, poverty, cultural context, culturally responsive teaching.
Describe and support the idea of relevant curriculum in a global context. Including knowledge of state standards and current educational system reforms.
Identify the procedural and practical aspects in the day to day life of an elementary educator.

Discuss and support through research relevant educational topics such as gender, equal opportunity, social class, race and school achievement, legal implications of teaching, school effectiveness, curriculum development, child guidance and classroom management, children with special circumstances, roles of teachers, diverse neeeds of students, professionalism etc.
Compare and contrast traditional and non-traditional methods of instruction and evaluate the benefits and limitations of each

rows.title: Cultural Geography
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze geographic patterns of income, urbanization, resource consumption, population growth, and access to education, healthcare, drinking water, and food within wealthy (most developed), middle income (developing), and poor (least developed) countries.
Compare and contrast origin areas (cultural hearths) of major world religions and languages with modern distributions of major world religions and languages.
Assess human rights within selected countries and regions, including the rights of women, ethnic, and religious minorities, immigrants, aboriginal peoples, and LGBTQ+ populations.
objectives: Compare and contrast environmental determinism, eco-feminism, and human ecology as modes of analyzing human-environment relationships.
Differentiate folk and popular culture.
Distinguish among formal, functional, and vernacular culture regions.
Analyze the general distribution of population across the surface of the Earth, emphasizing relationships between density, development, and economic activity.
Examine the dynamic origins of agriculture, including the relationships between early agriculture and the origins of cities.
Construct a general historical geography of the Industrial Revolution, including technology systems.
Categorize the world distribution of the major languages and religions.
Distinguish between political geography and geopolitics.
Differentiate among traditional patterns of urban structure, including North American cities, European Cities, Latin American Cities, Islamic Cities, and cities in the developing world.
Evaluate the unevenness of economic development across the globe.
Analyze the differential impact of climate change on wealthy and disadvantaged populations.

Evaluate the socioeconomic status and political representation of historically marginalized groups, including women, ethnic and religious minorities, immigrants, aboriginal peoples and LGBTQ+ populations.

rows.title: First Aid/CPR/AED For Non-Medical Professionals
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Complete a certification in First Aid/CPR/AED for adults and children
Make decisions and take appropriate steps to keep a victim alive and alleviate injuries until advanced medical services arrive.
Follow safety procedures that will promote calmness in emergencies
Render life saving assistance to: a. Adults b. Children c. Infants
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe how to recognize an emergency and size up the scene.
Understand legal concepts as they apply to lay responders, including consent and the purpose of Good Samaritan laws.
Identify how to reduce the risk of disease transmission when giving care.
Demonstrate how to check a person who is responsive for life-threatening and non-life-threatening conditions.
Explain how to check an injured or ill person who appears to be unresponsive.
Recognize the signs and symptoms of a heart attack, and describe appropriate first aid care for a person who is showing these signs and symptoms.
Demonstrate CPR and use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) for a person who is in cardiac arrest.
Demonstrate first aid care for a person who is choking.
Recognize the signs and symptoms of shock, and describe appropriate first aid care for a person who is showing these signs and symptoms.
Recognize the signs and symptoms of, and describe appropriate first aid care for, the following sudden illnesses: breathing emergencies, diabetic emergencies, seizures, fainting and stroke.
Describe methods used to control external bleeding, including the application of direct pressure and the application of a commercial tourniquet.
Demonstrate the application of direct pressure to control external bleeding.

Recognize the signs and symptoms of, and describe appropriate first aid care for, the following injuries: burns; muscle, bone and joint injuries; and head, neck and spinal injuries (including concussion).
? Recognize the signs and symptoms of, and describe appropriate first aid care for, the following environmental injuries and illnesses: heat-related illnesses, cold-related illnesses and poisoning.

rows.title: Basic Firefighter Physical Fitness
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate the ability to participate in a physical fitness program, including both anaerobic and aerobic activities.
Improve or maintain one's current fitness level.
Perform a variety of fitness drills related to standardized testing for Firefighters.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate the ability to follow standardized team disciplined drills.
Demonstrate the ability to participate in a physical fitness program, including both anaerobic and aerobic activities.

Participate in training which requires a) the ability to lift objects weighing a minimum of 50 lbs. from the ground to a minimum shoulder height; b) hand eye coordination; c) leg strength and coordination; d) grip strength; e) arm and upper body strength; f) correct body weight distribution and g) shoulder strength.

Successfully complete the follwoing stations of the physical agility test within the required individual and cumulative times: hose stack, stair climb, obstacle course, hose drag, and hose reposition.
Define health.
Discuss at least four reasons why disease prevalence has changed over time.
Differentiate between changeable and non-changeable risk factors.
Identify at least four behavioral risk factors associated with cardiovascular disease and cancer.
List at least two behavioral risk factors associated with osteoporosis and hypertension.
Identify normal values for total cholesterol and LDL, VLDL, and HDL-cholesterol components.
Describe at least four ways to lower total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol.
Describe at least four ways to raise HDL-cholesterol.
Define the following terms: nutrition, nutrients, nonessential nutrients, essential nutrients, calories, vitamins and minerals.
Describe the caloric content in 1 gram of carbohydrate, protein, fat and alcohol.
Analyze factors that influence personal food choices.
Describe the components of the food pyramid.
Describe serving sizes for each food category.
Describe the function of carbohydrates, fiber, protein and fat.
Describe at least three differences between simple and complex carbohydrates.
Calculate grams of fat, saturated fat, protein and carbohydrates, given total daily calories.

Develop a 1-day menu that satisfies the minimum standards of the food pyramid, incorporates variety and quality (low in fat, saturated fat, cholesterol and sodium and high in fiber, nutrients and monounsaturated fat).

Using food labels, calculate the percentage of calories from fat, protein and carbohydrates; figure grams of complex carbohydrates and grams of monounsaturated fat and interpret percent of daily values.
Define the following terms: metabolism, basal metabolic rate, total caloric expenditure, total caloric intake, overweight and obesity.
Describe at least five factors that affect metabolism.
Describe at least two problems associated with low calorie diets.
Calculate total calories burned in a given day.
Describe each health-related fitness component.
Describe acute adaptations to exercise.
Describe chronic adaptations to exercise.
Define interval training.
Differentiate between aerobic, intermittent and anaerobic activities.
Describe five factors that affect flexibility.
Compare and contrast target heart formulas and the talk test.

rows.title: Introduction to Marketing Principles
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will be able to demonstrate a significant understanding of the fundamental concepts of accounting, business law, economics, communication, and marketing.
Students will be able to produce clearly written, concise analyses, and deliver clear, well-organized, persuasive oral presentations.
Students will be able to use accounting information to make informed decisions about the internal operations of a company.
Students will be able to demonstrate an understanding of the role planning, organizing, leading and controlling plays in organizational success.
Students will be able to identify and apply ethical principles in management decision making.
Students will be able to describe what marketing entails and shows how the components are implemented.
Students will be able to analyze, interpret and present economic data.

Students will demonstrate their understanding of the role digital technologies play in the success of organizations and will demonstrate proficiency in the use of digital technologies by solving business problems using those technologies.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will be able to evaluate the place and contribution of marketing to the business enterprise.

Students will be able to define primary and secondary sources of information; give examples of methods used to collect primary data; give examples of sources for secondary data; compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of both types of data.

Students will be able describe major bases for segmenting consumer and business markets; define and be able to apply the three steps of target marketing: market segmentation, target marketing, and market positioning; understand how different situations in the competitive environment will affect choices in target marketing.
Students will be able estimate the costs and benefits of marketing channels; discuss the firms and the functions involved in typical channels in North America.
Students will be able illustrate how the international trade system, economic, political-legal, and cultural environments in a foreign country affect a company’s international marketing decisions.

Students will be able identify the roles of advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling, and direct marketing in the promotion mix; compare and contrast integrated marketing communications with a non-integrated approach to the promotional mix

rows.title: Fundamental Skills in Music
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and notate Western pitches by letter name and on a music staff
Construct scales idiomatic to Western Common Practice Era music
Construct triads idiomatic to Western Common Practice Era music
Translate basic written notation to the piano keyboard, and notes on a keyboard to notated music
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and explain the basic elements of notated music in the Western Common Practice Era tradition.
Notate and read pitches in multiple clefs.
Read scale patterns and chords.
Translate basic written notation to the piano keyboard.
Identify and construct time signatures.
Identify and construct key signatures.

rows.title: Personal and Social Adjustment
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will demonstrate a broad understanding of the dynamics of change and choice throughout the lifespan, and reflect on the efficacy of their own life choices.
Students will relate concepts and perspectives associated with personal and social well-being to their own lives.
Students will apply theories of human development to personal and social growth and change.
Students will apply methods and approaches to conducting psychological research, as well as hone their ability to read and evaluate research studies in the discipline.
Demonstrate skills necessary for college success, including planning, time management, and short/long term goal setting
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify contemporary issues in adjustment.
Compare and evaluate research methods used in psychology to examine adjustment including case studies, interviews, survey methods, quasi-experiments and laboratory experiments and correlations.
Compare and evaluate ethical issues in adjustment research.

Differentiate and evaluate the major psychological perspectives associated with personality and adjustment including trait approaches, biological approaches, psychoanalytic approaches, learning approaches, cognitive approaches, and humanistic approaches.

Evaluate the major concepts associated with stress including sources of stress, types of stress, physical reaction to stress, psychological reactions to stress, and individual differences in stress response.

Evaluate the major concepts associated with coping including definitions of coping, effective coping strategies, ineffective coping strategies, cultural, individual, and personality influences on coping.

Evaluate the major issues associated with development of the self-concept and identity including self-esteem, self-attributions, moral development and values, identity development, and cultural influences on self-concept and identity formation.

Distinguish the major concepts related to social cognition and adjustment including attitudes and behavior, person perception, persuasion, conformity and obedience, resisting social influence, and intergroup relations.

Distinguish the major issues associated with interpersonal communication including verbal and nonverbal communication, listening skills, speaking skills, self-disclosure, barriers to effective communication and enhancing communication.

Evaluate the major issues associated with gender and adjustment including contemporary perspectives on gender roles, gender stereotypes, gender similiarities and differences, development of gender identity and sociocultural influences on gender concepts.

Differentiate and evaluate the major concepts in human sexuality that impact adjustment including human sexual response, sexual knowledge, attitudes and behavior, sexual harassment, rape, sexual assault, child sexual abuse, and sexually transmitted diseases.

Describe and compare the major issues associated with interpersonal relationships including attraction and friendship, intimate relationships, jealousy and loneliness, lifestyle variations, family violence, and cultural influences on relationships.
Distinguish and evaluate the major issues associated with adult development including the family life cycle, parenting, personality development in adulthood, aging, and death and dying.

Distinguish and evaluate the major issues associated with careers including career development, career exploration and planning, job satisfaction, work-related stress, changes in the workplace and the workforces, and leisure.

Describe and compare the major issues associated with abnormal behavior including definitions of abnormality, anxiety disorders, mood disorders, schizophrenia, personality disorders, substance-use disorders, biological and cultural influences on disorders, and legal issues and disorders.

Describe and compare the major concepts associated with the treatment of disorders including psychoanalytic therapies, humanistic therapies, behavior therapies, cognitive therapies, biological therapies, group therapies, community psychology, guidelines for seeking therapy, effectiveness of therapies, and sociocultural issues and therapy effectiveness.

Distinguish and evaluate the major issues associated with health including historical perspectives on health psychology, promoting healthy lifestyles, coping with illness, substance abuse and addiction, and cultural influences on health.
Design a research project, collect empirical data, analyze the data, and compare the data to contemporary research and theory in child and adolescent psychology.
Compose and analyze a multi-source research paper on an issue in child and adolescent psychology employing appropriate research techniques and documentation in APA format.

rows.title: Introduction to Statistics
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Describe and summarize data of samples and populations.
Correctly apply the addition or multiplication rules of a probability experiment.
Correctly evaluate probability from a binomial or normal distribution.
Correctly define and conduct a hypothesis test.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:
Assess how data were collected and recognize how data collection affects what conclusions can be drawn from the data.
Identify appropriate graphs and summary statistics for variables and relationships between them and correctly interpret information from graphs and summary statistics.
Describe and apply probability concepts and distributions.
Demonstrate an understanding of, and ability to use, basic ideas of statistical processes, including hypothesis tests and confidence interval estimation.
Identify appropriate statistical techniques and use technology-based statistical analysis to describe, interpret, and communicate results.
Evaluate ethical issues in statistical practice.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Recognize the proper use of statistics and distinguish them from the abuse of statistics.
Distinguish among different scales of measurement and their implications.
Apply concepts of sample space and probability.
Apply proper rules of probability.
Identify and understand the methods of data collection while evaluating the quality and appropriateness of the data.
Describe, analyze, and summarize the data of samples and populations, using numerical and graphical summaries.
Calculate measures of central tendency and variation for a given data set.
Calculate the mean and variance of a discrete distribution.
Calculate probabilities using normal and t-distributions.
Construct and interpret confidence intervals.
Compare and contrast different kinds of probability distributions, including the binomial, the uniform and the normal, and select the correct distribution in applications.
Run various tests of hypotheses on various types of sample statistics, while appropriately using the Central Limit Theorem.
Apply techniques of linear correlation and regression of bivariate relations.
Determine and interpret levels of statistical significance including p-values.
Identify the basic concept of hypothesis testing including Type I and II errors.
Select the appropriate technique for testing a hypothesis and interpret the result.
Formulate hypothesis tests involving samples from one and two populations.
Use linear regression and ANOVA analysis for estimation and inference, and interpret the associated statistics.
Interpret the output of a technology-based statistical analysis.
Compare and contrast applications from business, psychology, sociology, life science, health science, education and other disciplines.
Correctly use statistical technology (software such as Excel or MINITAB) to calculate and display descriptive statistics of samples and populations.
